questions.prompt: Which training approach is Claude built on, according to the 'What is Claude?' lesson?
choices: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback only
questions.explanation: The lesson names Constitutional AI as the approach that guides Claude to avoid toxic outputs, refuse to help with illegal or unethical activity, and behave as a safe and beneficial AI. See: Claude 101 → What is Claude?

questions.prompt: On which plans is Claude available, as listed in 'What is Claude?'
choices: Free, Pro, Max, Ultra, Team and Enterprise
questions.explanation: The lesson states Claude apps are available to all plan types: Free, Pro, Max, Ultra, Team and Enterprise. See: Claude 101 → What is Claude?

questions.prompt: What is Claude's default context window size, and what is the maximum available on paid plans with supported models?
choices: 200K default, around 1 million on Pro, Max, Ultra, Team and Enterprise
questions.explanation: The lesson gives 200K tokens (about 500 pages) by default, with up to 1M tokens available on Pro, Max, Ultra, Team and Enterprise plans using supported models. See: Claude 101 → What is Claude?

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT listed as a way to access Claude in the 'What is Claude?' lesson?
questions.explanation: The lesson lists Claude.ai, Claude Code, Claude Tag (Slack), Claude Design and Claude for Microsoft 365. There is no Claude for WhatsApp. See: Claude 101 → What is Claude?

questions.prompt: The lesson describes a three-part frame for a good prompt. What are those three parts, in order?
choices: Setting the stage, defining the task, specifying rules
questions.explanation: The lesson frames a good prompt as: set the stage (role and context), define the task (what Claude should do), and specify rules (style, tone, examples). See: Claude 101 → Your first conversation with Claude.

questions.prompt: Which file types does the lesson list as supported for upload?
choices: PDF, DOCX, CSV, TXT and common image formats (PNG, JPEG)
questions.explanation: The lesson lists PDF, DOCX, CSV, TXT and common image formats (PNG, JPEG) as supported upload formats, including charts and graphs inside PDFs. See: Claude 101 → Your first conversation with Claude.

questions.prompt: Which Claude model does the lesson describe as the recommended default for everyday use?
questions.explanation: The lesson calls Sonnet 'the best choice for everyday users and our recommended default model'. Opus is for the most complex tasks. See: Claude 101 → Your first conversation with Claude.

questions.prompt: How do you refine a request you have already sent, without starting a new chat?
choices: Delete the conversation and begin again
Start a new chat and paste the old prompt
Click the pencil icon on your message, edit it, and resubmit
questions.explanation: The lesson says you can click the pencil icon on any of your messages to edit and resubmit — useful when you want to refine your request rather than add a new message. See: Claude 101 → Your first conversation with Claude.

questions.prompt: Where do personal instructions that apply to every conversation live, and what are they called in Settings?
choices: Settings → search for 'Instructions'; this is called Your Claude preferences on mobile
There is no such setting — instructions only apply to one chat
questions.explanation: The lesson's pro tip: click your name, open Settings, and search for Instructions; on mobile go through Your Claude. What you write there applies to every conversation. See: Claude 101 → Your first conversation with Claude.

questions.prompt: A reply comes back too generic. What does the lesson tell you to try first?
choices: Ask Claude to be more creative
Add details about your audience, role and constraints
questions.explanation: For a generic reply, the lesson says your prompt did not include enough context: add details about your audience, your role and your constraints. See: Claude 101 → Getting better results.

questions.prompt: What do the four letters of the 4D Framework for AI Fluency stand for?
questions.explanation: The 4D Framework identifies Delegation (what to hand to AI), Description (how to prompt it), Discernment (judging the output), and Diligence (using AI responsibly). See: Claude 101 → Getting better results.

questions.prompt: The lesson describes a simple way to test Claude on your own work before you rely on it. What is it called?
choices: An eval — comparing Claude's output to examples you already know are right
A dry run in Research mode
questions.explanation: An eval is a lightweight check: gather 5–10 past examples where you know the right answer, prompt Claude, compare. See: Claude 101 → Getting better results.

questions.prompt: You got a confident answer that turned out to be wrong. What does the lesson recommend?
choices: Verify key facts yourself; ask Claude to cite sources or confidence; use web search to ground the answer
Switch to Haiku for safer replies
Accept that AI makes mistakes and move on
questions.explanation: For high-stakes work the lesson says to verify key facts independently, ask Claude to cite sources or indicate confidence, and use web search to ground responses. See: Claude 101 → Getting better results.

questions.prompt: The lesson describes three 'shapes of work' with Claude on the desktop. Which group is correct?
choices: Turn by turn, handing work off, building software
questions.explanation: Lesson 4 defines the three shapes as turn by turn (Chat), handing work off (Cowork), and building software (Code / Claude Code). See: Claude 101 → How you work with Claude on your desktop.

questions.prompt: What is the clearest practical difference between Chat and Cowork in the lesson?
choices: Chat uses Sonnet, Cowork uses Opus
Cowork can read local folders and save files back; Chat reads uploads but hands results back as downloads
Chat is free; Cowork is paid
questions.explanation: The lesson spells out that Cowork can read a folder on your computer and save finished work back to it; Chat reads uploads but returns downloads. See: Claude 101 → How you work with Claude on your desktop.

questions.prompt: Scheduled tasks and subagents are features of which shape of work?
questions.explanation: The lesson lists scheduled tasks and subagents under Cowork — the hand-off shape. See: Claude 101 → How you work with Claude on your desktop.

questions.prompt: A task has several steps, needs files saved to specific folders, and should run every Monday. Which shape fits best?
choices: Building software in the Code tab
questions.explanation: Multi-step, outputs are files in your file system, and runs on a schedule — the lesson's three reasons to hand work off to Cowork. See: Claude 101 → How you work with Claude on your desktop.

questions.prompt: What does a Claude Project store, that a plain chat does not?
choices: Instructions, a knowledge base of files, grouped chats, and memory specific to the Project
questions.explanation: A Project is a self-contained workspace with its own chats, instructions, knowledge base and memory. See: Claude 101 → Introduction to projects.

questions.prompt: Your Project knowledge base grows past the context window. What does Claude do?
choices: Refuses to answer until files are removed
Switches to RAG — searches your Project files and brings in only the relevant parts, raising effective capacity about 10x
questions.explanation: The lesson explains Retrieval-Augmented Generation: Claude searches the Project's knowledge and brings in only what is relevant, expanding capacity by up to 10×. See: Claude 101 → Introduction to projects.

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT a Project permission level in Team/Enterprise plans, according to the lesson?
questions.explanation: The lesson lists three permission levels: Can view, Can edit and Owner. Comment-only is not one of them. See: Claude 101 → Introduction to projects.

questions.prompt: You upload a one-off file during a chat inside a Project, but do not add it to the knowledge base. What happens?
choices: It is added to the knowledge base automatically
It stays available only in that chat, separate from Project knowledge
It is lost after the next message
It is shared with every member of the organisation
questions.explanation: The lesson spells this out: a file uploaded in a single chat stays separate from the Project knowledge base and is only used in that chat. See: Claude 101 → Introduction to projects.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a good Project practice from the lesson?
choices: Give every file the same generic name so Claude is not biased
Name files descriptively (for example Q4-2026-Brand-Guidelines.pdf) so Claude can find and reason over them
Upload every company file you own, 'just in case'
Keep instructions blank and let Claude learn from use
questions.explanation: The pro tip in the lesson: descriptive file names help Claude retrieve the right content. See: Claude 101 → Introduction to projects.

questions.prompt: What is an artifact in Claude?
choices: A finished output — a document, deck, design, chart or interactive page — that opens in its own window and lives in the Artifacts tab
questions.explanation: The lesson defines an artifact as a stand-alone output in a dedicated window beside the chat, saved separately in the Artifacts tab. See: Claude 101 → Creating with artifacts.

questions.prompt: Which of these are the three dedicated artifact types the lesson names for common deliverables?
choices: Claude Pages, Claude Sheets, Claude Boards
Claude Design, Claude Slides, Claude Docs
Claude Flows, Claude Mail, Claude Mockups
Claude Write, Claude Draw, Claude Chart
questions.explanation: The lesson names Claude Design (visual work), Claude Slides (presentations) and Claude Docs (living documents). See: Claude 101 → Creating with artifacts.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between an artifact and file creation?
choices: File creation is paid; artifacts are free
An artifact opens inside Claude and is shared by link; file creation gives you a downloadable file you open in another app (Word, Excel, PowerPoint, PDF)
Artifacts are only for code; file creation is for everything else
Artifacts are permanent; files are temporary
questions.explanation: The lesson distinguishes them clearly: an artifact opens and updates in Claude and is shared by link; file creation hands you a file to download and open elsewhere. See: Claude 101 → Creating with artifacts.

questions.prompt: Three ways to change an artifact once it exists, according to the lesson. Pick the correct set.
choices: Delete and remake; export and re-import; undo
Edit it directly, comment on the piece you want changed, or ask in the chat
Only through the conversation; direct edits not supported
Only by uploading a new version
questions.explanation: The lesson lists three ways: edit directly, comment (optionally @-mentioning Claude), or ask in the chat. See: Claude 101 → Creating with artifacts.

questions.prompt: A chart or diagram inside a Claude Doc shows numbers from a connected tool. Does it update by itself?
choices: No — it is a snapshot; ask Claude to refresh it when you need the latest numbers
Only if you set a refresh schedule
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly says charts and diagrams in a Doc are a snapshot, not a live feed; ask Claude to refresh. See: Claude 101 → Creating with artifacts.

questions.prompt: On a Team or Enterprise plan, can an artifact be shared with someone outside your organisation by default?
choices: Yes, every artifact is public by default
Yes, with a 'view' link, but not with 'edit'
No — external sharing is off until an Owner turns it on in Organization settings → Artifacts
Only if the recipient has a Claude account
questions.explanation: Links stay inside the organisation by default. External sharing is available only after an Owner enables it. See: Claude 101 → Creating with artifacts.

questions.prompt: What is a Skill in Claude?
choices: A folder of instructions, scripts and resources that Claude loads automatically to perform a specialised task well
questions.explanation: The lesson defines Skills as folders of instructions, scripts and resources that Claude loads dynamically for specialised tasks. See: Claude 101 → Working with skills.

questions.prompt: Which setting must be ON for Skills to work?
choices: Create and edit files (also called Code execution and file creation)
questions.explanation: Skills need Create and edit files turned on because they run in the sandboxed computing environment. On Team and Enterprise this is an organisation-level setting. See: Claude 101 → Working with skills.

questions.prompt: What is the easiest way to create your own custom Skill, according to the lesson?
choices: Hand-write the SKILL.md file in a text editor
Talk to Claude about the workflow you want to repeat; Claude interviews you and generates the skill file
Buy one from the Skills store
questions.explanation: The lesson says the easiest route is a conversation with Claude: you describe the workflow, Claude interviews you, and it generates the skill for you. See: Claude 101 → Working with skills.

questions.prompt: Skills vs Projects — which contrast is right?
choices: Projects store process, Skills store knowledge
Projects store knowledge, Skills define a process Claude executes
They are the same thing with different names
Skills are for teams, Projects are for individuals
questions.explanation: The lesson contrasts them: Projects are knowledge hubs, Skills are procedural machines (process). A skill can reference knowledge from a project. See: Claude 101 → Working with skills.

questions.prompt: Why does the lesson advise you to install only custom Skills from trusted sources?
choices: Because a Skill can include executable code
Because Skills can see all your memory
questions.explanation: Skills can contain executable code, so the lesson warns to only install from trusted sources and review what a custom Skill does before using it. See: Claude 101 → Working with skills.

questions.prompt: What is the open standard that powers Claude's connectors?
questions.explanation: The lesson names MCP (Model Context Protocol) as the open standard behind connectors — 'USB-C for AI'. See: Claude 101 → Connecting your tools.

questions.prompt: Which of these statements about connectors is TRUE?
choices: A connector lets Claude browse your data on its own, without being asked
Claude can only see what you can see in the connected service; disconnecting revokes access
Connectors are only for Enterprise plans
Only one connector can be active at a time
questions.explanation: The lesson spells it out: Claude sees only what you see, and you can revoke access by disconnecting or through the service's own security settings. A connector gives a request somewhere to point; it does not go hunting on its own. See: Claude 101 → Connecting your tools.

questions.prompt: You want to use Claude with Jira. Which connector entry should you look for in the directory?
choices: Atlassian — covers both Jira and Confluence
questions.explanation: The lesson uses this exact example: one Atlassian entry covers both Jira and Confluence. See: Claude 101 → Connecting your tools.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a web connector and a desktop extension?
choices: A web connector works only on the web, a desktop extension works only on the desktop
A web connector links Claude to a cloud service through sign-in; a desktop extension runs locally through the Claude desktop app and reaches local files or native apps
A desktop extension is paid, a web connector is free
questions.explanation: The lesson distinguishes them clearly: web connectors for cloud services, desktop extensions for local files and native apps on your computer. See: Claude 101 → Connecting your tools.

questions.prompt: Research mode in Claude is designed for what kind of task?
choices: A multi-angle investigation across many sources that returns a cited report, typically five to forty-five minutes
A one-shot summary of a single document
questions.explanation: Research breaks a complex question into sub-questions, explores hundreds of sources, and returns a cited report, usually in 5–45 minutes. See: Claude 101 → Research for deep dives.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a Claude surface built on top of a Microsoft 365 app?
choices: Claude for Microsoft 365 (sidebar in Excel, PowerPoint, Word and Outlook)
questions.explanation: Claude for Microsoft 365 appears as a sidebar inside Excel, PowerPoint, Word and Outlook. See: Claude 101 → What is Claude? and Other ways to work with Claude.

questions.prompt: You keep re-explaining the same brand guidelines and re-uploading the same style guide to Claude. Which feature should you use?
choices: A Project with the guidelines in its knowledge base and the rules in its instructions
questions.explanation: The lesson names this pattern exactly: when you re-upload the same files or re-explain the same rules, a Project is the fit. See: Claude 101 → Introduction to projects.
